title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan
subtitle: How the Internet stopped handing out addresses in three fixed sizes and started counting prefix bits.
summary: CIDR replaces the old Class A, B and C network sizes with prefixes of any length, written like 192.168.99.0/24, where the number after the slash says how many leading bits name the network. Addresses are handed out in blocks that follow provider-customer relationships, so a provider can advertise one aggregate route instead of thousands. Routers pick the matching route with the longest prefix. This 2006 Best Current Practice replaces the original CIDR spec, RFC 1519, and reports on twelve years of deployment.

eli5.summary: Instead of selling street addresses only in three fixed sizes, the Internet began cutting them to fit, and gave each neighborhood one big sign so the mail carrier needs only one line in his notebook.

questions: what does the slash mean in an ip address
what is the difference between cidr and subnetting

tldr.problem: Class A, B and C addresses came in only three sizes, so the Class B space was running out and the global routing table was growing faster than routers could cope.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses are written as a prefix plus a length (a.b.c.d/n), allocated in power-of-two blocks along provider lines, and summarised by providers into aggregate routes. Routers forward on the longest matching prefix.
tldr.outcome: CIDR eased the routing-table and Class B crisis in the 1990s and is how IPv4 routing still works. The RFC itself calls it a short-term fix that has far outlasted its expected lifespan.

lineage.title: How IPv4 addresses and routes got classless

today: Every IPv4 router and operating system today works with prefixes and prefix lengths; the slash notation is in routing tables, firewall rules and cloud network settings. BGP-4 (RFC 4271) carries the prefix length with every route, and IPv6 address architecture uses the same prefix-length notation. The pressures this document describes have not gone away: the global table still grows as sites multi-home and de-aggregate for traffic engineering.

implementations.note: The ip route command installs and shows routes as prefix/length, forwarding by longest match.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4632 describes the strategy for assigning the existing 32-bit IPv4 address space so that it is used sparingly and so that the growth of global routing state stays under control. It obsoletes the original CIDR specification, RFC 1519, with two aims: to clarify the concepts, and, after more than twelve years, to report how the technology worked out in deployment.

It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 122), not a protocol with a wire format. The document is about how addresses are named, who hands them out, and how routers are expected to summarise and forward on them.

The authors state that CIDR was intended to be a stopgap lasting about three to five years. It has become the mid-term solution and is still in use today.
sections.eli5: This is a note about how to hand out house numbers on the whole Internet so that we do not run out of numbers and the mail sorters do not drown in paperwork.

sections.title: The problem: three sizes only
sections.content:
Under the original plan in RFC 791, networks came in three classes, chosen by the leading bits of the address. Class A (leading bit pattern 0) allowed 128 networks of 16,777,216 addresses; Class B (10) allowed 16,384 networks of 65,536; Class C (110) allowed 2,097,152 networks of 254 usable hosts. The IETF set up the ROAD group in November 1991, which met in January 1992 and named three problems.

Class B exhaustion
Class C was too small for a mid-sized organization and Class B too big, yet Class B was the best fit available.
Routing table growth
Tables in Internet routers were growing beyond what software, hardware and people could manage.
Address exhaustion
The 32-bit space itself would eventually run out.

The RFC says CIDR addresses the first two and only eases the third, buying time for a longer-term solution.
sections.eli5: Imagine shirts sold only in tiny, medium and gigantic. Almost everybody picks gigantic, so those run out first, even though most of the shirt is wasted. Meanwhile the shop's catalog keeps getting longer.

sections.title: Classless addressing and prefix notation
sections.content:
CIDR drops the classes and makes explicit which bits name the network (the prefix) and which number hosts inside it. A prefix is written as an ordinary dotted address, a slash, and a decimal length from 0 to 32. The legacy Class B network 172.16.0.0 becomes 172.16.0.0/16; the Class C network 192.168.99.0 becomes 192.168.99.0/24.

Because the length is explicit, a block can be any power-of-two size from 1 to 232 addresses. A /15 holds 217 (131,072) addresses and a /21 holds 211 (2,048). The RFC's table also notes /32 as a host route, /31 as a point-to-point link and /0 as the default route.

Allocation follows a hierarchy. IANA hands /8 blocks to the Regional Internet Registries, which allocate or assign smaller blocks to Local Internet Registries and ISPs, who in turn pass pieces to customers. In registry terms, to allocate is to delegate space for further sub-delegation, while to assign is to give it to a site that numbers its own hosts.
sections.eli5: The slash number says how many digits at the front are the street name. The rest of the digits are the house. A short street name means a long street with lots of houses. A long street name means a tiny street.

sections.title: Aggregation and distributed assignment
sections.content:
The only commonly understood way to shrink routing state, says the RFC, is aggregation, and aggregation only works if addresses follow the network topology, which in practice means following service providers. A customer numbered out of its provider's block needs no route of its own; the provider advertises one aggregate for the whole block.

Two cases weaken this. A multi-homed site connected to several providers has to be advertised by each of them, so its global routing cost is about what it was before CIDR. A site that changes provider without renumbering "punches a hole" in the old provider's aggregate, so the new provider advertises a more specific route, which wins because it is a longer match. The RFC recommends that such sites eventually renumber.

Assignment itself was decentralised. A single central registry had been the bottleneck, so delegation began, first to RIPE NCC in Europe, and is now a hierarchy of IANA, the RIRs and providers.

The RFC says there is no hard requirement for an end site to renumber when changing provider. It encourages doing so to avoid explicit advertisement of its prefix.
sections.eli5: If everyone on Maple Street gets a number from the Maple Street block, the post office only needs one line, "Maple Street goes this way." A house that moves to Oak Street but keeps its old number needs its own special line.

sections.title: Routing rules
sections.content:
Without classes, the mask can no longer be guessed from the first bits of an address, so prefix lengths must be carried explicitly. OSPF, IS-IS, RIPv2, EIGRP and BGP-4 all do this. Older protocols such as RIP (RFC 1058), HELLO, IGRP and EGP do not, and the RFC says they should not be used in transit networks on the global Internet.

Rule 1: longest match
Forwarding is by longest match. So a multi-homed destination must always be advertised explicitly into the routing domain above it, never hidden inside an aggregate.
Rule 2: discard route
A router that generates an aggregate must discard packets that match the aggregate but none of its more-specific routes, typically by installing a null route. This prevents forwarding loops.

Other practices follow. The mask must be contiguous. The default route 0.0.0.0/0 must be accepted by all implementations, but should be advertised to another routing domain only if explicitly configured. Route filters must accept masks, and aggregation is normally configured by the AS that owns the block, or by a provider on its behalf. The RFC urges extreme caution with proxy aggregation, because it can shift traffic in ways other networks do not expect. Transit networks must use iBGP to carry routes learned from other providers.
sections.eli5: When a sorter has two signs that fit a letter, "Maple Street" and "12 Maple Street", he follows the more exact one. And if he is told "all of Maple Street is mine" but can't find the house, he throws the letter away instead of sending it back up the road to be sent here again.

sections.title: Worked example: providers PA and PB
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a provider, PA, holding 524,288 (219) addresses from 10.24.0.0 to 10.31.255.255, which is 10.24.0.0/13 and equals 2,048 old Class C networks. PA connects six sites in order: C1 (/21), C2 (/20), C3 and C4 (/22 each) and C5 and C6 (/23 each). A seventh site, C7, moved to PA but keeps the block 10.32.0.0/20 from PB's space (PB holds the next 2,048 /24s). C4 is multi-homed with PA primary and PB secondary; C5 is primary through PB and secondary through PA. Both providers connect to a backbone, BB.

By rule 1, PA must advertise its aggregate, C7 and C4. PB advertises its aggregate, C5 and C4. The diagram below shows what BB hears. A packet for 10.24.12.9 matches PA's /13 and the /22 for C4, and the /22 wins.

The example also shows an operational wrinkle. If PA loses C7, BB drops the /20 and sends C7-bound traffic to PB's less specific /13, where rule 2 discards it. Nothing is broken, since C7 is unreachable anyway, but traceroute will point at PB.
sections.eli5: Two big post offices each shout their own neighborhoods to one central sorting room. Some houses are shouted by both, and for those the sorting room picks the one with the more exact address.

sections.title: What CIDR did to the routing table
sections.content:
Section 9 of the RFC reads the "Active BGP Table Entries" graph in eight stretches. There was exponential growth until about 1994, when no aggregation was possible and each new site meant new routes. A sharp drop followed in 1994 as BGP-4 let providers aggregate supernet blocks. Roughly linear growth lasted from mid-1994 to early 1999. Then came a new exponential period around the high-tech bubble, driven in part by more-specific advertisements for multi-homing and traffic engineering. Growth flattened with the dot-com bust and the "CIDR police" campaign for better aggregation, and returned to a linear rate in 2002 and 2003. Exponential growth had resumed from 2004.

As of March 2005 the base aggregate load was some 75,000 entries, and about 85,000 more were more-specific routes inside that base.

The RFC criticises providers that de-aggregate on purpose, for example to counter hijacking, as fundamentally non-scalable. It also notes many advertise both an allocation and every /24 inside it.

Its conclusion is that without better multi-homing and traffic-balancing technology, aggregation is the only tool available to make routing scale.
sections.eli5: Once everyone used big signs instead of one note per house, the notebook shrank. Then people started adding extra notes for special cases, and it began to grow again.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names two concerns that longest-match forwarding makes worse. First, hijacking: anyone who advertises a more specific prefix than the one normally announced pulls traffic toward themselves. Its example is a provider advertising 192.168.16.0/20, with a malicious operator advertising 192.168.17.0/24 to divert a host at 192.168.17.100. The RFC notes spammers have used this to hide where mail came from.

Second, denial of service by route flooding, where a large number of routes overflows routing and forwarding tables. The "AS 7007" incident, a misconfiguration and not an attack, is its example of this failure.

Remedies are trust relationships between providers and strict route policy filters. Because such filters are hard to build in a decentralised Internet, many providers set limits on how long a prefix they accept, based on RIR allocation sizes, and a cap on the number of prefixes accepted from each neighbor. The RFC says this is not an exhaustive analysis.
sections.eli5: If the sorter always follows the most exact sign, a prankster can post a very exact fake sign and steal your mail. So post offices have to check who is allowed to put up which signs.
